author: buchanan_robert
cushag
text:
It is so long since I went down into this valley!

How sweet its air was, and how smooth its stream rolled,

How lovely all the hill sides that closed around me—

The sun shone bright on the purpled heather,
Like little stars were the daisies dotted,
The gorse like flame against the sky burned,
But never shall I forget when they brought me back again
That wretched little white room, without door or window,
Where I lay sick, and knew no joy but that which you gave me.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
“Ah, now we have no little boys!” said my sister.
The thought came as I sat down on her sofa—
So long I had not seen my brother’s children!
“Yes,” answered my friend, “they are gone away from us.”
Then suddenly there shot through me an inspiration;
For I remembered that they were both so small,
My younger brother and his wife, when their first child
Came home to visit them one winter evening;
How he put up a footstool for his daughter,
That she might sit in the firelight at

author: buchanan_robert
text:
Then came I out where the wind blew free,
Into the clear cold light of day;
For a long time no birds sang me cheer,
But I went on my way alone.

author: cushag
text:
He he ! she he!

Weel, this is my story.

It happened on Tuesday night—a young fellow and his missis was havin' their supper; they was talkin' about the weather, you see, when along come a gentleman with a lady in tow. He asked if it wasn't lovely out there; so they all went to window and saw that the moon looked like it was tryin' to eat the clouds up; then one of them said the wind was blowing strong off shore. Well, the two gentlemen, bein' fond o' sailin

author: emily_dickinson
text: " Ma-ry, ma-ry. ma- ry, min d’ chil !”

I don't see why you are so downhearted. It ain't as if it were a case of death or sickness that you had to bear with fortitude and patience. You have only got to go away from home a little while and then come back again when you feel better. You wouldn't think what a change there would be in one's feelings; but such is life-a series of changes. Don't say anything about going away. When we get enough money together we will take a trip somewhere— perhaps to Europe—to look at the sights. They do them

author: cushag
text:
We had a young feller come here to see me —

I knowed him well enough,

But we didn't think that he would ever be married ;

So much his looks did tell.

He sat down on my bed and said he liked it;

Said he thought it looked so neat—

"For when you have been in such places as this," says he,

"They never make no more use o' beds."

author: cushag
text:
I can hear her now
She comes runnin' through the door.
" Mary dear, where have you been?
Mother said to buy some butter."

author: emily_dickinson
text:
They do not know that they are gone,
 The children who play there;
 They have no thought that when their feet
 Go over this way,
 It is our hope that they will come,
 Their voices we hear;
 And for us on the other side
 We pray, while we wait here.

author: john_keats
text:
I love to be among the woods
 The trees are standing so straight;
 It makes me think that man is good,
 That he was made as they were made.

I thought that he would say "How long"
Or "When will you come home?"
But only his hand came round my head,
And kissed me again and then withdrew;
He stood before me like a dream,
His eyes looked strangely at me too,
The very thing that makes one glad
Is always something new.

Still another:

The days are all alike now -
There's no change from day to day.
The sun looks pale through mist and snow,
While cold winds sing their wild refrain,
As they blow along the leafl

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I am a bird upon your window,
 I sing for joy;
 For in the garden grows a lily,
 That blooms no more than I.

You may think that this is an easy task, but it isn't so simple as it seems. One girl in our class wrote about her sister, who had been taken away from home by death: "I am sad because she has gone." Another child wrote how his father loved him with all his soul, yet he felt sometimes that the world was against him. A boy wrote about his mother's work; she cared not only

author: emily_dickinson
john_keats
text:
The sun shone bright in the east; yet on my face
Its rays were lost, as when some cloud beneath
Hides from the moon the sky's azure blue;
Till rising high, and far above the place
Whereon I stood, it broke into sudden blaze,
Like one who enters suddenly his house,
Whose door was open wide for years of age.

author: john_masefield
text:
The house-door opens; out goes the dog,
With mouth in air, tail streaming from him long:
Up leaps a page, with shining buckles girt;
He bows before us as we enter in,
To let the way for my lord the host.

I've heard it said many times before
The old man never left his door;
That when he did come out at night,
His lantern shone all day-light.

Then on we went as if the sun were blind,
Along the road 'twixt town and country-side—
Over the grass-grown highway where we trod—
And down beneath the shadow of the wood;
Until, in sight of the garden gate,
We met an ancient dame, who looked like fate,
With her large face drawn up into a frown,
Who

author: john_keats
text: It was midnight, or rather the first cock-crow; when from my window I beheld the pale moon shining on the distant sea, where its bright beams were reflected in millions of tiny sparkling diamonds, which shot up here and there into clouds of brilliant glory. The whole night had been dark, but this moment a change came—the sky cleared, and an inky darkness filled it. Suddenly as if struck with lightning, the stars burst out! They blazed like gems thrown from heaven’s rich treasury. The deep blue sea became alive with their rays; for every wave glittered like a

author: john_keats
text: There is no need of many words for describing these wonders; but this I must observe—that the king was in high spirits when he saw it, which made him more gay than ever at being there.—He seemed as if he had never been out of his kingdom before, or heard of any thing like these places. He gave all the people presents of gold, silver, clothes, &c., and sent them home very happy.—

author: john_masefield
text: "One day he told his sons that he had been ill for months. 'I must leave my money to a good cause,' he said. He gave each son half what he owned and put the rest in a savings bank where it could do no harm."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
"Then I went home in a dream-like state,
As though all things had been done for me.
My head was clear when I left school at last,
For my education took its start then."

"The man who gave my soul a home
Has gone for ever from his throne;
Gone out of life into that unknown
To which so many have returned;
For in the midst of this dark hour
There came an angel, bearing power.
He said "Thy work is done," and then
He left him in eternal peace.
Farewell!"

author: john_masefield
text:
"What did he see in this? That she was a lady,
That he should never meet again at the mill.
He didn't care much for what came after;
But that he might not grow too proud or dull--
Or not be thought a fool because of his youth--
He felt obliged to do as he was told."

author: john_masefield
text:
"The boys are getting together in my room
To practise some music. I don't mind it so much,
For this is a holiday from school; but the rest
Of the family think they have lost their rights."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
The great ship moves on without delay, . . ,
Her sails are set. . ., And she is making way

For lands across the trackless deep;
Yet my heart yearns for home again, . ..

I long to see it where my fathers sleep,
On the dear shores where we were born—
To watch the sunset burn its light

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I would sail on the seas all my life long;

I am young, and strong and healthy-minded,

But there is something in this world that kills,

Which I must find out before I grow too old

And blind to see it, deaf to hear it —

What do they call it?

God gives good gifts unto his children; so it seems.
He gives us our bread, and wine with cheese and meat;
But if he would take this world away from me,
I think He’d not give me back my sight nor speech!

Yet here I am, though in my latter days,
To write a verse or two for some young lad;
What have they done that I should care to write,
Save I have written verses many years ago
For other lads who lived before me died?

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
The waves are wild as dogs! The wind is in my face;
I fear to look behind me to see what’s chasing me.
For all their power and violence they give no rest;
They beat upon me with angry hands, and yet
Their teeth are cold, their fingers hard as stones.
If ever they should get control, if ever one should dare
To break against me—to crush me—then I hope
That Death may take his revenge and carry off my soul!

My life is not so good, though it seems good here,
In this

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text: The sea is not just water with air on top of it; the sea has been made in a very careful way; people who are living there also work hard to keep it clean so they will have food and other things for their daily life. We must love our oceans because it gives us many resources such as fresh drinking water, fish, etc. So we should always do something good for them or else they may get polluted which will affect marine life and humans too.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I shall not live to see the year’s end; for
the wind is now cold and stiffly blowing

In wintertime when I was but little child.

author: robert_frost
newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
In those days there were no highways; for there
was not one man that had an ox nor an ass to draw
his cart over the rough uneven ground. They went
on foot along the narrow paths, or they laid their
burden on beasts like oxen and asses; but in
wintertime they used sledges. And when the weather
was cold, sometimes as much snow lay upon the earth
as it does now here in summer. So Christ Jesus, who
went up into heaven, preached good news unto men.

And another by the unknown author:

So it was

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
And all thy sins are washed away in blood divine;

All thy sins that make thee guilty and unclean,

author: robert_frost
text:
"The man came in the house one day,
And all my life seemed very strange;
It had been quite so before—but now
It did not seem as if I were home

author: stephen_crane
text:
"The boy works for nothing; we'll keep him here
Till he wants something more than wages, then
We can make something out of him for less
Than if he had been born in our own family—
Which would not do at all. I hate people
Who come along with ready money—so much easier
For them to teach. If we take this one,
We shall never get rid of him again.'"

"The workhouse gate is shut; we are in here,
We are in no more. If you find them poor
And half starved, don't leave them out to perish;
Bring them home again, but bring them as guests.

author: robert_frost
text:
"We were sitting round the kitchen table,
At supper in our clean white shirts,
Talking about old times; I said: "It must be
You are talking now to my mother—
Your own dear mother." He looked away
And shook his head—his voice began to shake—
"I had no mother," he said. There was silence
For some minutes. Then he got up and went
To bed, saying not a word. The next day
He left me without another word.

author: robert_frost
text:
"Here is a man," says his wife to me,
"Who has come up from Cornwall in search of work;
The farm where he used to live is sold now
And they are all going down to London town,
Except this one—he couldn't leave behind
His mother and father and sisters three."
"Is he working for you?" "No! He hasn't yet
Found anything suitable or well paid."

author: stephen_crane
text:
As I sat down at my desk, there was one of those unexpected flurries of inspiration which are not so infrequent as you might suppose. It had been snowing heavily all day and I could see nothing out of doors but drifting flakes; so with a smile on my face I began to write down the lines which followed almost immediately. They were these:-

"The wind is rising fast--the night is blackening round me-
 I hear no sound save the creak of door behind me-"

I went on like this for several pages till suddenly I saw before me the figure of a

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The two brothers who died at sea,
 Each had a sister whom they loved;
 One was tall and one was short,
 And one was fair and one brunette.

And this:

When I say my name is John,
 There's nobody on earth will know it so soon as you!

One day I sat on my doorsteps and heard a bird singing, singing so loud. It was not the song of one bird, but a company of them. One bird after another came forward. The singing rose higher and higher till it reached its highest note, then all together they sang as if there had been only one. It seemed like music in my ears. At first I thought this could be no other than an echo coming from some hill top or distant forest; but as they kept up the strain for hours without any pause, I began to wonder whether these singers might really live here on

author: stephen_crane
text: I've heard it said there is no greater love than one from father to daughter. I think otherwise, for if you ask my mother she will tell you all about our friendship and how we talk every day on the telephone or when I come home from work; then after dinner if there's time she always comes into my room and tells me all her troubles and asks me what I think about them so we both feel better afterward. She told me once she had tried killing herself but didn't have any nerve enough because she was afraid it would spoil my life. That makes me think it

author: stephen_crane
stothert_james_a
text:
This is the Soul, and thou art one With her ;
For she hath no form or figure fair :
She's but a thought of beauty, and so clear
That even the dullest sense can bear.

author: thomas_hardy

text:
The sun of Nature sheds his rays on earth;
From whence their beauty and delight diffuse :

Our life-blood throbs ; for, round him placed, we rest,

Each moment gathering sweetness from his bliss.

For, though a thousand things, that make us sad,

Are found within the world’s bright circle cast,
Yet joys more numerous are around us spread,

That soothe us in affliction—while we taste.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
How like a garden I am found!
Though little plants and flowers there be,
They are not wanting of their food;
The sun's hot rays do cheer them through.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The Great Creator and His works of Love are one —
One God, One Nature, one great Cause,

In whom and through Whom we all have life :

This Life eternal, which no death can quench,
Of which the Earthly Man was born, and died ;

That He might live again, from out his grave,
To be at last a glorified Spirit Man —

No more subject to decay, corruption and disease.

author: thomas_hardy
text: I am not one who likes to leave the world behind me when I die, or go where it is impossible to return. The other day my wife showed me an old poem which I had written some years ago. It was called “The Passing Bell” (thereby indicating that the subject was death), but although its form was formal, it was also very much of a personal nature. At any rate, it gave me quite an idea of how things are put away, just before going on their way to Eternity. Perhaps you may like to read them?

author: william_wordsworth

text:
I WISH they were all that I have dreamed!
 To make my heart’s delight complete:
 I could not be without them yet.
 For they are always with me.

 My home is like the world beyond:
 There are things good, evil too;
 But none can change or touch the sound
 That keeps me happy through and through.

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I saw them pass before me, 
Them that went not back again,
With laughter in their faces,
Their souls full up to heaven.

It seemed they neared an opening 
Where some new world shone afar:
And I thought, if I could only 
Have lived my little span out so!

author: thomas_hardy
william_wordsworth
text:
In vain was she so long oppressed; in vain
 Did all our efforts, day by day, grow less;
 And every effort seemed but like another strain
 Of death upon Death; until at last we ceased

author: buchanan_robert
text:
All hail, thou happy Isle! when first I saw
 Thy soft waves from their long course gently draw
 To greet me in their arms, and softly wave,
 While I looked on them from afar amazed;
 When, having reached their goal, they roundly lave
 The shore whereon I stand,—what other land

When shall these mournful shades remove? when cease
 The long arrears of death and woe? When, O
 How welcome, will return the blessed years,
 Which were our country's brightest hours? And then
 What will become of us, whom Fate has led
 To seek in other climes for peace or bread?
 Or will they still remain like orphans here,
 Without a friend, without a home, without prayer?

author: william_wordsworth
text:
What are those shadows? - they will pass away.
 What are those forms? - ah! these are things I know;
 These are my friends - now gone for evermore,
 Now in their graves, whose silent tombs lie low,
 And from this world, where all our hopes have flown,
 To Heaven above no more return again.

I read a passage in an old book about 'The English Poets', which gave me the impression that Shelley was only a very mediocre poet. The author then went on to say that he had some beautiful lines, but these were rare indeed

author: william_wordsworth
text:
Where’er thou look'st, where e'er thou go'st ,
 No sight so sweet can meet thine eye ;
 The earth in joy was born to know
 Her lord from God had come for aye.
